articles.title: Fake vacation rental sites use live chat to steal your data
articles.summary: Fortra researchers say fake vacation rental sites use live customer support chats to trick travelers into handing over credit card details this holiday.
articles.body: You're booking a vacation rental for the holidays when a message appears saying there's a problem with your reservation. Before you can figure out what's wrong, a customer support chat opens and offers to help. You're told your credit card won't be charged, but you'll need to enter the number to complete a security check. Sounds helpful, right? That's exactly what scammers want you to think. Cybersecurity researchers have uncovered fake vacation rental sites that look remarkably similar to legitimate booking platforms. Some even include live customer support chats designed to convince travelers to hand over their credit card information. With Thanksgiving travel approaching, it's worth knowing how these scams work before you book your next trip. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. FAKE BOOKING.COM TRAVEL CREDIT SCAM TARGETS TRAVELERS Fake vacation rental sites are getting harder to spot Researchers with Fortra's Intelligence and Research Experts (FIRE) team recently identified fraudulent travel-booking websites that impersonate popular vacation rental platforms. The scammers copy legitimate property listings and surround them with details you'd expect to see on a real booking site. You might recognize the familiar layout or see reviews that make a property seem trustworthy. The photos may even come from an actual vacation rental. One example uncovered by researchers showed listings for an apartment and a house. Both appeared to be legitimate properties available for booking. Someone searching for a holiday rental could easily spend more time comparing the accommodations than questioning the website itself. That's the problem. A professional-looking listing tells you very little about who's actually running the website. Fortra says its researchers identified and remediated examples of these phishing sites. The company did not report how many travelers may have fallen for the scams or whether money was stolen. Fake booking messages make travelers think something went wrong The scammers also know that travel plans can be stressful, especially around the holidays. If you've already arranged transportation and suddenly see a warning about your accommodations, you're probably going to want answers. Researchers found fraudulent booking pages displaying messages such as: In one case, a fake booking page told visitors their reservation was still unconfirmed. To finish the process, they needed to complete what the website called a mandatory verification step. The page reassured them that there would be no additional charge. But the next screen asked for personal information, including contact details that scammers could potentially use for future phishing attacks. Researchers also identified a separate website impersonating a major lodging platform. Its login page used recognizable branding and familiar sign-in options to encourage visitors to submit account information. That creates another risk. If you use the same password for multiple services, giving it to a fake booking website could put those other accounts in danger. Fake customer support chats make the scam more convincing The live chat feature is what makes this scam particularly concerning. In a separate case, Fortra's researchers discovered a fraudulent travel-booking page with a credit card payment form and a live support chat. When visitors expressed concerns, the chat responded and described the card request as a routine security check. It even reassured visitors that their cards wouldn't be charged. Now consider how often you've used an online customer support chat to straighten out a billing problem. You explain what's happening, someone responds and you follow their instructions. Most of the time, that experience is perfectly legitimate. Scammers are borrowing that familiar interaction to make their websites seem more trustworthy. The chat's reassurance was designed to encourage visitors to submit payment details. The researchers did not say whether a real person or an automated system operated the chat. Either way, the conversation was part of the fraudulent booking process. And that's an important reminder. Just because someone responds to your questions in real time doesn't mean you're dealing with the company you think you're dealing with. FAKE E-ZPASS EMAIL THREATENS $100 FINE OVER UNPAID TOLL Tips to protect yourself from fake vacation rental sites Before you enter your credit card information or book a place to stay, take a moment to make sure you're dealing with a legitimate website. A little extra checking now could save you from losing money or having your personal information stolen. 1) Go directly to the official booking website If you're using Airbnb, Vrbo or another rental platform, open its official app or enter the website address yourself. Don't rely on links in unexpected emails or text messages, even when they mention a reservation you recognize. Be cautious with sponsored search results as well. Scammers sometimes pay for advertisements that lead to fraudulent websites. If you're unsure about a booking message, go back to your account through the official platform and look for it there. 2) Look closely at the website address A fake website may use a familiar company logo while hiding behind a completely unrelated web address. Scammers also add extra words to brand names to make fraudulent domains appear legitimate. Check the address before signing in or entering your credit card number. Remember that a padlock symbol doesn't guarantee a website is safe. It only indicates that the connection is encrypted. 3) Verify the property before paying Found a rental you really like? Search for the address separately and see whether the property appears on another reputable booking website. Compare the details and pay attention to prices that seem unusually low. You can also reverse-search the listing photos to see where else they're being used. However, finding matching photos doesn't automatically prove the listing is legitimate. Scammers often steal pictures from real properties. Take a few minutes to read reviews from previous guests. If something about the listing doesn't add up, contact the booking platform directly. 4) Don't let an urgent warning rush you If a message claims your reservation will be canceled unless you act immediately, check your booking through the official website or app. A legitimate reservation problem may require attention, but that doesn't mean you should trust a link that arrived unexpectedly. If the warning doesn't appear in your account, contact customer support using the information published on the company's official website. 5) Keep your payments inside the booking platform Be especially careful if a host asks you to visit another website to complete payment. The same goes for unexpected requests to move the conversation to WhatsApp or another messaging service. Airbnb warns that paying outside its platform can leave guests without AirCover protection. Vrbo also requires bookings and payments to follow its authorized process. Some legitimate properties may collect certain disclosed charges separately. If that happens, confirm the payment instructions through the official booking platform before sending money. 6) Protect your devices with strong antivirus software Strong antivirus software that includes malicious website and phishing protection can help warn you about known fraudulent booking pages. Some security programs can also detect suspicious links before you enter sensitive information. Keep your browser updated as well, since updates often include important security fixes. Of course, newly created scam websites may escape detection. Security software helps, but you still need to check where you're entering your information. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com. 7) Pay with a credit card when possible Credit cards generally offer stronger protections for disputing fraudulent charges than many other payment methods. That's especially useful when you're paying for an expensive vacation rental. Be suspicious if someone insists on a wire transfer or wants payment through cryptocurrency. Gift card requests are another major warning sign. Once money is sent using these methods, recovering it can be difficult. Even when paying by credit card, make sure you're using the actual booking platform. 32 TRAVEL ESSENTIALS THAT HELP PROTECT YOU AND YOUR BELONGINGS THIS HOLIDAY SEASON 8) Be careful with identity verification requests Some legitimate vacation rentals require identification. However, that doesn't mean you should upload your driver's license or other sensitive documents to an unfamiliar website. If you're asked to complete an unexpected verification process, confirm it through your official reservation. Also, never share a one-time security code with someone contacting you through a support chat or message. That code could give a scammer access to your account. 9) Use a password manager and two-factor authentication A password manager can help you recognize a suspicious login page. If the website address doesn't match the saved address for your account, the password manager generally won't autofill your credentials. That doesn't automatically prove the site is fraudulent, but it's a good reason to check the address more carefully. Use unique passwords for your booking accounts and enable two-factor authentication. Passkeys are another good option when a service supports them. What to do if you've entered information on a fake rental website If you think you've shared personal or financial information with a scammer, act quickly. Here's what to do based on the information you provided. Kurt's key takeaways I think the live chat feature makes this scam especially troubling. We're so used to turning to customer support when something goes wrong that we tend to trust the person offering to help. And that's exactly the reaction these scammers are hoping for. I wouldn't assume a booking website is legitimate simply because someone in a chat window tells me everything is fine. My advice? If you're asked to enter your credit card information to fix an unexpected reservation problem, stop and check with the booking company directly. I know that's frustrating when you're trying to get your holiday plans settled. But I'd rather spend a few extra minutes verifying a reservation than find out later that a scammer has my credit card number. Have you ever had a vacation rental reservation suddenly require additional payment or verification? Did you trust the request, or did something make you suspicious? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com. Sign up for my FREE CyberGuy Newsletter CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Copyright 2026 CyberGuy.com. All rights reserved.

articles.title: Senate further advances bipartisan permitting reform bill
articles.summary: The Senate took a series of key votes on Wednesday to advance a permitting reform bill that seeks to speed up the nation’s ability to build infrastructure and energy. The upper chamber advanced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) 65-31 in a procedural vote known as a cloture vote, helping it move toward…
articles.body:
The Senate took a series of key votes on Wednesday to advance a permitting reform bill that seeks to speed up the nation’s ability to build infrastructure and energy.

The upper chamber advanced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) 65-31 in a procedural vote known as a cloture vote, helping it move toward final passage and overcoming the Senate’s 60-vote threshold.

This is not a surprise, as the legislation has also advanced in other recent votes, though it represents the formal clearance of a key hurdle to the bill becoming law.

While there were enough votes to pass, it appears some support has been dropping off. A vote early last week, for example, passed 73-25 .

Sens. Josh Hawley (Mo.) and Mike Rounds (S.D.) were the only Republicans to vote against the legislation Wednesday. Rounds had previously voted against the bill, citing disagreement with some of the bill’s provisions on power lines . Hawley previously voted to advance debate on the bill, but he opposed the bill in a procedural vote earlier this week.

The Democrats and their caucusers who voted against the legislation were Sens. Angela Alsobrooks (Md.), Tammy Baldwin (Wis.), Michael Bennet (Colo.), Richard Blumenthal (Conn.), Lisa Blunt-Rochester (Del.), Cory Booker (N.J.), Maria Cantwell (Wash.), Catherine Cortez Masto (Nev.), Tammy Duckworth (Ill.), Dick Durbin (Ill.), Maggie Hassan (N.H.), Mazie Hirono (Hawaii), Tim Kaine (Va.), Mark Kelly (Ariz.), Andy Kim (N.J.), Ben Ray Luján (N.M.), Ed Markey (Mass.), Jeff Merkley (Ore.), Patty Murray (Wash.), Jon Ossoff (Ga.), Alex Padilla (Calif.), Gary Peters (Mich.), Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), Jeanne Shaheen (N.H.), Tina Smith (Minn.), Chris Van Hollen (Md.), Elizabeth Warren (Mass.), Peter Welch (Vt.) and Ron Wyden (Ore.)

The measure is still expected to go through an amendment process as some lawmakers have insisted on tweaks, including addressing concerns from tribes that its changes to historic preservation law don’t give them adequate input into projects that may impact them. It’s not clear whether these or any other amendments will make it into the bill’s final text.

The legislation seeks to address long-standing gripes from developers that the U.S.’s environmental review and other processes pose significant hurdles to the nation’s buildout.

Its supporters say the bill will help the American economy and bring down its planet-warming emissions at the same time through significant benefits for renewable energy.

Opponents warn, however, the BAAJA could be bad for the environment as it bolsters fossil fuels and mining, loosens environmental laws and limits the ability of a project’s opponents to challenge it in court.

Among those opponents are several environmental groups and tribes. The bill is supported by a wide array of industries, including those representing renewable power, fossil fuels, manufacturing and chemicals. It’s also supported by major labor unions.

While the bill appears highly likely to pass the Senate, its path in the House is a bit less certain. It has bipartisan House support, but it faces some opposition from progressive Democrats. Meanwhile, House Energy and Commerce Chair Brett Guthrie (R-Ky.) has raised pieces of the bill he’d like to change .

It is competing with a crowded lame-duck agenda that includes a lapse in federal funding in December if Congress does not act. But the bill has support from the White House, which could help push it through.

The legislation seeks to boost the nation’s ability to build power lines, which is particularly key to helping renewable energy projects get onto the grid, including by allowing federal regulators to approve the lines if states don’t act on them.

It also contains provisions that seek to prevent presidents from yanking existing permits from energy of all types — combating President Trump’s ability to block already-approved wind projects and moves made by Democratic presidents, such as revoking approval from the Keystone XL pipeline.

The bill also allows project developers to sue the government if they can demonstrate a pattern of disparate treatment of certain energy sources.

The BAAJA also exempts certain activities, including expansions to natural gas pipelines, from environmental reviews and limits those reviews to only alternatives that meet the goal of a project’s sponsor company.

It restricts lawsuits against projects by mandating that they be filed within 150 days of a project’s approval and only allows people who weighed in during a formal public comment period to sue.

The bill also seeks to rein in increased electricity costs from large data centers, forcing them to pay for any costs stemming from their high electricity demand. However, these facilities may also benefit from the general provisions that seek to help industry build.

articles.title: Trump’s latest land grab is an AI hub in the Philippines
articles.summary: To secure chips and critical minerals for AI, the US is turning to a former colony.
articles.body: President Donald Trump was greeted by no less than five beauty queens when he landed in the Philippines on Tuesday, according to local news outlet Rappler. As he stepped onto the tarmac, a child handed him small US and Philippine flags. A band played “YMCA,” a staple at Trump rallies, as more girls in traditional bell-sleeved blouses and young men in wide-brimmed hats danced to the song. Outside the airport, hundreds of protesters packed streets bearing signs — and at least one prop casket — saying “Trump out.” Others say “Reject Pax Silica,” the name for the US-led international initiative to secure chips and critical minerals used in the hardware fueling the AI boom. “Pax” comes from the Latin word for “peace, stability, and long-term prosperity,” the Pax Silica website proudly says. Yet the unspoken question — peace and prosperity for whom? — explains the whiplash between the Philippine government’s warm welcome of Trump and the public fury raging outside. Trump says he wants to “win AI” — whatever that means. As such, the US needs data centers full of GPUs to do it. With Americans increasingly opposed to data centers and chip factories being built in their communities, the US is now recruiting less affluent nations to take up some of the slack. Lawmakers from both the US and the Philippines are promising a slice of the riches that advances in generative AI are supposed to create. And that’s supposed to be worth the land razed, homes destroyed, and natural resources lost in the name of technological progress. In the Philippines, that’s taking the shape of a proposed 1,620-hectare (4,000 acres) hub for chip factories, processing plants for critical minerals, and data centers. At least two dozen countries have signed on to the Pax Silica initiative, and Trump was expected to pressure more to join while in the Philippines for events related to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit. With Pax Silica, the US aims to insulate itself from China’s dominance in manufacturing semiconductors and processing critical minerals needed to make those chips. Trump held a bilateral meeting with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. Wednesday before heading to Shenzhen to meet with China’s President Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin. Philippine and US officials are expected to sign a framework agreement by the end of the year for the jointly developed Pax Silica Economic Security Zone. The details are still murky and shrouded in NDAs. The Philippines’ Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) overseeing the plan expects an economic boom from minerals processing and chip manufacturing, with perhaps a data center or two on site. Meanwhile, human rights advocates who oppose the project warn that it will displace Indigenous residents, cutting them off from water resources on which they rely. “We do not want to give up our community,” Petronila Capiz-Muñoz, chieftain of the Indigenous Aeta Hungey tribe, told Human Rights Watch. “How do we give up our burial grounds, our church, our livelihood? This is where we source our water, this is where we plant.” Capiz-Muñoz said BCDA officials have told residents that they’ll need to relocate by December to make way for development. Small farmers are also afraid the semiconductor hub will push them off their lands, according to Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch. There are layers of land-grabbing to unpack here. The Aeta are among the first people to inhabit the Philippines, believed to have arrived around 30,000 years ago. And yet the Aeta Hungey tribe has been trying since 1994 to secure an official certificate recognizing its ancestral domain in one of the areas now facing industrial development. But since the tribe hasn’t been granted that certificate, the BCDA can still claim the AI hub will be built “outside titled ancestral domains.” The agency says the project will be on public land located at the former Clark Air Base built in the early 1900s when the Philippines was a US territory. The Philippine constitution now only allows its own citizens to own private land. But the BCDA can offer leases lasting as long as 99 years to foreign developers. The agency expects to rake in close to $1 billion USD (about 60 billion in PHP Peso) from lease income over the first 25 years. The BCDA was in talks with around 30 different companies interested in setting up shop in Clark’s proposed AI hub, then-BCDA President and CEO Joshua Bingcang told reporters in July. He couldn’t name names, he said, because of NDAs — creating the same kind of opacity that has turned Americans against data centers on their home turf. He did mention, however, that an American energy company was conducting a feasibility study into building a liquefied natural gas (LNG) line and plant to meet the hub’s enormous electricity demand. Bingcang called LNG a clean fuel, but that’s provably false. LNG is primarily methane, a smog-forming pollutant that is an even more potent greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide. Bingcang said in September that the Philippine government wanted to invite Nvidia, TSMC, and Apple. While one or two data center developers had expressed interest, according to Bingcang, most of the companies interested were “high tech” manufacturing firms. He has also described chip manufacturing as a “clean” industry, echoing corporate spin that’s been around since the start of Silicon Valley. At the first chip fabs in California, workers — many of them Filipino immigrants — donned “bunny suits” to assemble sensitive chips in environmentally controlled “clean rooms.” Little did they know that the gear they wore offered little protection against the harsh chemicals used in manufacturing, which also leaked out of storage tanks to contaminate soil and groundwater. When studies came out in the ’90s documenting disproportionately high rates of miscarriages among workers, companies pledged to phase out some of the chemicals linked to reproductive health risks. Around the same time, chip manufacturing started to move out of the US to Asia, where similar health problems stemming from the same chemicals cropped up even decades later. Chipmakers say their fabs have gotten much safer over the years, in part because more work is automated. Even so, the BCDA estimates that the AI hub will create up to 190,000 direct jobs. The BCDA, White House, and Philippine’s Malacañang Palace did not immediately respond to questions from The Verge. “I don’t want to date myself, but I knew your parents very well. They were great,” Trump told President Marcos during his visit. Marcos’ parents are estimated to have stolen up to $30 billion from government coffers over decades of rule before a people power movement ousted the current president’s father from the same office in the 1980s. But public memory, it seems, can be short. And skyrocketing demand for more powerful chips used for generative AI has raised fears among environmental and labor groups that history might repeat itself. Companies move fast and break things, leaving a toxic mess in their wake. And when Americans decide they’ve had enough in their own back yards, the industry sets up shop somewhere else where they think their customers aren’t paying attention and politicians are happy to look the other direction.

articles.title: Lawmakers push for Medicare coverage of Alzheimer’s screening tests
articles.summary: Two lawmakers shared how they have personally been impacted by Alzheimer’s and pushed for bipartisan legislation that would provide Medicare coverage for early blood testing for this disease and other dementias during a Wednesday event hosted by The Hill. Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) and Rep. Nanette Barragán (D-Calif.) are both advocating for the passage of…
articles.body:
Two lawmakers shared how they have personally been impacted by Alzheimer’s and pushed for bipartisan legislation that would provide Medicare coverage for early blood testing for this disease and other dementias during a Wednesday event hosted by The Hill.

Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) and Rep. Nanette Barragán (D-Calif.) are both advocating for the passage of the Alzheimer’s Screening and Prevention (ASAP) Act .

Cramer reflected on his mother’s battle with Alzheimer’s in a pre-recorded interview shared at “The Promise of Early Intervention: The ASAP Act and A New Look at Life with Alzheimer’s” event, which was sponsored by HealthyWomen.

“Early diagnosis is better for treatment, for preparation, certainly even for possible cures,” he said. “We’ll get there hopefully soon and well with Alzheimer’s.”

The North Dakota Republican said there was a “financial case” to be made for legislation like the ASAP Act that would cover the costs of early screening measures.

“This is a prudent early investment that can save lots of money in the long run, whether it’s for nursing care to include in home or immersion home, just the preparation for families,” Cramer said. “I think there’s a message that cuts across the broadest of political swaths.”

The ASAP Act, which was introduced last year by Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), would authorize the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) to cover early detection blood tests that have been approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) under Medicare.

Barragán, who sits on the House Committee on Energy and Commerce’s Health Subcommittee, also expressed her support for Medicare coverage of these tests in an interview with The Hill’s contributing editor Kathleen Koch on Wednesday.

“Without having a Medicare cover and pay for this, it will be inaccessible to some folks,” she said in a pre-recorded interview shared at the event.

Barragán noted that the ASAP Act would also authorize CMS to cover new blood tests approved by the FDA, calling this provision a “game changer.”

The Democrat also shared her experience as a caregiver after her mother’s Alzheimer’s diagnosis.

“It took way too long for somebody to see if she had the symptoms and she was really at risk for Alzheimer’s, and so that’s one of the reasons I’m so excited when I hear about new developments, new tests and making sure everybody has access to new tests, because we should know as early as possible,” Barragán said.

articles.title: Texas reverses course on data center permits after Abbott pause
articles.summary: Texas environmental regulators have resumed reviewing data center permits after outgoing Gov. Greg Abbott ordered a pause on issuing new permits in September. In August, Abbott directed the state’s public utility commission (PUC) and its grid operator, ERCOT, to audit all data centers’ electricity and water use, saying authorities “must conduct a comprehensive verification and…
articles.body:
Texas environmental regulators have resumed reviewing data center permits after outgoing Gov. Greg Abbott ordered a pause on issuing new permits in September.

In August, Abbott directed the state’s public utility commission (PUC) and its grid operator, ERCOT, to audit all data centers’ electricity and water use, saying authorities “must conduct a comprehensive verification and audit of all data centers advancing through ERCOT’s interconnection process before any additional data centers are approved to move forward.”

Last week, the state’s Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) received notice from Abbott’s office that officials at ERCOT have completed gathering information on potential community impacts from data centers, the Texas Tribune reported Tuesday.

“The agency has resumed its normal permit review process and will evaluate applications under all applicable state and federal laws and regulations,” TCEQ spokesperson Laura Lopez said in a written statement according to the Tribune report.

In September, the governor sent a letter to TCEQ directing the agency to stop all permits to data centers until the ERCOT audit is completed, the Tribune reported . The same month, Abbott directed the Texas Water Development Board (TWDB) to penalize data centers that fail to enforce state water-use reporting requirements.

President Trump previously has maintained his stance on supporting data center development, saying it would be “a mistake” to push back on data centers.

“I’m not taking positions,” the president told Punchbowl News . “I just think it’s a mistake because there are other communities that want it. When a community wants it, it means a lot of money is going to come into that community.”

The debate around data centers was in focus in the days leading up to the midterm elections, as many candidates campaigned on stricter regulations.

Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa (D) was one such candidate who vowed to establish a moratorium on data center construction .

Following the elections, Hinojosa, who defeated Abbott in the midterm elections, reiterated her promise to protect Texans from data center projects, saying, “what has happened is data centers have moved into mostly rural communities, and there are no rules and laws to protect Texans, and Texans are being taken advantage of.”

articles.title: Fed minutes: Officials favored holding rates steady in October, but they see hikes ahead
articles.summary: Almost all members of the Federal Reserve favored raising interest rates in the future, even as they decided to hold rates steady in October, according to mi...
articles.body:
Almost all members of the Federal Reserve favored raising interest rates in the future, even as they decided to hold rates steady in October, according to minutes from the central bank's last policy meeting released Wednesday.

"With regard to the outlook for monetary policy in the months ahead, almost all judged that, under their baseline outlooks for inflation and the labor market, further action to raise the target range for the federal funds rate — broadly consistent with the September Summary of Economic Projections — would likely be appropriate, in order to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2% objective," the minutes, which are released with a three-week lag, revealed.

The September Summary of Economic Projections, which includes 18 officials' expectations for the path of interest rates — excluding Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, who doesn't pencil down his — showed one more rate hike this year, then holding rates steady throughout 2027.

Among those who favored holding rates steady at the last meeting, many said they wanted to gather additional information to help determine the best level of interest rates to bring inflation back down to their 2% goal in a timely way. These officials wanted to assess the durability of AI-related investment demand, the evolution of financing conditions, the transmission of the September rate increase to the economy, and geopolitical developments.

Some said that market expectations for rate hikes in December and next year were broadly consistent with their views on the path of interest rates, and several saw this alignment as reducing the risks of keeping the target range unchanged in October. A few felt holding rates steady was a close call.

Some participants favored raising rates at the last meeting, citing inflation remaining too high with few signs of it abating. They thought rates weren't high enough to restrict the economy and cool inflation, and a few warned that further delay risked allowing high inflation to become entrenched or necessitating a larger and more disruptive tightening later. Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack, a voting member who publicly dissented last meeting, has made this argument. Fed governor Lisa Cook also dissented last meeting.

Several officials observed that the impact of tariffs on prices appeared to be waning, but most remarked that inflation pressures in the economy were broad-based. The vast majority noted that high energy prices continued to contribute to inflation pressures.

articles.title: Murkowski joins Democrats in concerns about Project 2025 author’s nomination to be Interior watchdog
articles.summary: Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) joined Democrats in raising concerns about President Trump’s unusually political pick to lead the Interior Department’s nonpartisan watchdog office during his confirmation hearing on Wednesday. Murkowski raised objections brought by the department’s last inspector general (IG) — whom Trump fired in a purge of such watchdogs last year — to his…
articles.body:
Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) joined Democrats in raising concerns about President Trump’s unusually political pick to lead the Interior Department’s nonpartisan watchdog office during his confirmation hearing on Wednesday.

Murkowski raised objections brought by the department’s last inspector general (IG) — whom Trump fired in a purge of such watchdogs last year — to his new nominee for the role, Dennis Kirk.

Kirk’s nomination has proved particularly contentious because he has held political positions, including in the White House Office of Personnel Management during Trump’s first term. He was also a co-author of one of the chapters of Project 2025, the controversial blueprint for a conservative administration written by the Heritage Foundation.

“The former inspector general, Mark Greenblatt … I just want you to respond to a comment that he has made about your nomination. This is your opportunity to tell us why you think you should deserve to get this job,” Murkowski told Kirk during Wednesday’s Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee hearing.

“His quote is: ‘Inspectors general must be able to investigate the administration that appointed them without fear or favor. Mr. Kirk’s political background and close ties to this administration make it impossible for him to credibly meet that fundamental test.’” the senator continued.

She added that inspectors general play a “critical role” that must be done with “an unbiased view, impartiality, looking at what you have in front of you without tipping the scale one way or another with political favor.”

In response, Kirk said, “If confirmed, I guarantee you that I will implement absolutely independent oversight, excellence, integrity, and accountability.”

“The IG has the obligation to identify the risks, the vulnerabilities that impact all of the things that happen. To complete this mission, I commit to doing that exact thing: performing audits, investigations, evaluations, and giving those reports to Congress directly,” he added.

If every Democrat opposes the nomination, it could still pass with up to three Republicans in opposition. It is unclear whether Murkowski will ultimately oppose Kirk or whether other Republicans might join her.

If he has any shot at confirmation, Republicans will have to advance and vote on his nomination before Democrats retake the Senate majority in January.

He will face another hearing along with a slate of other nominees before the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on Thursday.

Greenblatt told The Hill that “it certainly seems like they are going to try to jam him in” with the back-to-back hearings.

During the Energy and Natural Resources hearing, several Democrats raised concerns similar to Murkowski’s.

Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii) asked the nominee if he would reassure lawmakers that he would do his job “without fear or favor?”

“I really enjoy what I do. I do it for everybody. I have served six presidents, including multiple other party presidents. I’ve never had a problem from any president I’ve served, or objections, or being accused of being political,” Kirk said.

“I think it is very clear that you are working for a president who expects loyalty. Would you agree with that?” Hirono said.

“I would hope everybody who serves the president under our Constitution remembers that the taxpayers and the Constitution allowed people to get people into office, and under our system, we vote for the person who makes policies and promises,” Kirk said.

“Excuse me, but you are working for a president who does not believe that the rule of law applies to him,” Hirono replied.

Kirk indicated he has not had such experiences and has never met Trump.

“Do you not watch the news or read the papers?” Hirono asked. “It is very clear that this president does not believe the rule of law applies to him.”

Meanwhile, citing a report that officials hold tech investments while pursuing data centers on public lands, Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.) asked, “As a person who would be in charge with preventing that waste, fraud, abuse and mismanagement, looking at inappropriate conflicts of interest, would it be your obligation to open an investigation into whether employees of the Interior Department are financially benefiting from the investments they have in these data management companies?”

In response, Kirk said, “It is our office’s position to identify those kinds of risks and look at those kinds of questions and I have a very trusted staff and I think that as those things come up to us, you can…be assured we will look independently and objectively at all that.”

“So that’s a yes, you will investigate it?” Cortez Masto asked.

The nominee said he couldn’t “commit” to the investigation, but he would “in good faith, be responsive to those questions and look at things that arise to those kinds of issues that are waste, fraud, abuse of the public fisc. I am a fiscal budget transformation kind of a guy. I am concerned about the taxpayer dollars.”

“Good. So am I, and that even includes this administration if they’re abusing taxpayer dollars. You’d be willing to look into that?” Cortez Masto continued.

Possibly confusing her question for a statement, Kirk replied, “Thank you.”

“OK. Thank you, a nonanswer,” Cortez Masto said.

After the hearing, Greenblatt called Kirk’s performance “uninspiring.”

“He mouthed the words of independence, but it seemed like an afterthought more than a core commitment,” the former inspector general said.

He had previously raised concerns the appointment could jeopardize the independence of the watchdog’s investigations and could compromise the identities of whistleblowers.

articles.title: Cybersecurity expert: ‘There will be a significant ramp up in incidents’
articles.summary: Jen Easterly, the former director of the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, on Monday warned that the U.S. will likely see a “significant ramp up” in incidents involving digital infrastructure, including outages and cyber threats. “We have to be prepared for disruption, because disruption is going to occur, so we need to plan for…
articles.body:
Jen Easterly, the former director of the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, on Monday warned that the U.S. will likely see a “significant ramp up” in incidents involving digital infrastructure, including outages and cyber threats.

“We have to be prepared for disruption, because disruption is going to occur, so we need to plan for it, prepare for it, exercise against it, have contingency plans in place,” Easterly told CNN ‘s Anderson Cooper.

She added that “at the other end of it, we will be able to have more secure and resilient infrastructure, but I am concerned that over the next few months and years, there will be a significant ramp up in incidents, and we don’t have all of the resources to be able to handle it.”

Easterly called for more “investment in the modernization of our infrastructure” that should be consistently sustained from one presidential administration to the next.

The interview comes after a near-daily rash of widespread outages and digital disruptions over the past week, raising questions about potential vulnerabilities to large-scale cybersecurity.

Apple saw technical issues with iCloud and Apple Pay following an “internal update” on Tuesday. The National Security Agency (NSA) also saw an outage that brought internal communications to a halt following “scheduled routine maintenance.”

On Monday, J.P. Morgan Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo saw disruptions preventing customers from accessing their bank accounts. United Airlines experienced a system outage also on Monday that resolved later in the evening.

The Federal Aviation Administration implemented a nationwide ground stop last Friday, the third in the agency’s history, believed by investigators to have been caused by a router needing an upgrade at a radio facility in Arkansas.

Microsoft experienced an hour-long global outage affecting 100,000 users and cut off access to Outlook between last Thursday and early Friday.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNBC on Tuesday that, amid public speculation, cyberattacks were not behind these outages.

“What I think is going on here, and I think there’s both a good news aspect to this and an aspect that we need to be clear-eyed about, is many people are patching their systems,” he said. “They know that they’re legacy systems, have vulnerabilities, they’re outdated … it is time for an upgrade across our digital infrastructure.”

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin suggested that super intelligence (SI) — the administration’s preferred term for artificial intelligence –– could have caused these outages, saying he spoke with a person in tech who thought “that it’s the SI.”

President Trump downplayed these incidents , telling reporters while in the Philippines that “it’s fine.”

“When you’re big and powerful and have all the money, things like that happen,” he said ahead of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit.

articles.title: NIH to move remaining retired research chimps to sanctuary
articles.summary: The National Institutes of Health (NIH) announced Wednesday it will release the last government-owned research chimpanzees in early 2027 to a sanctuary, ending a decade-long effort to get the animals out of federal laboratories. The 34 chimpanzees, currently housed at the Keeling Center for Comparative Medicine and Research in Bastrop, Texas, will be transferred to…
articles.body:
The National Institutes of Health (NIH) announced Wednesday it will release the last government-owned research chimpanzees in early 2027 to a sanctuary, ending a decade-long effort to get the animals out of federal laboratories.

The 34 chimpanzees, currently housed at the Keeling Center for Comparative Medicine and Research in Bastrop, Texas, will be transferred to Chimp Haven, a 200-acre Louisiana sanctuary that serves as the official retirement home for the government-owned apes, the NIH said.

“Completing their transfers will fulfill NIH’s commitment, announced in November 2015, to retire all NIH-owned chimpanzees to sanctuary,” NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya said in a statement.

Bhattacharya added the timing of the transfers, which are expected to begin early next year, will be “guided by the chimpanzees’ health, welfare and social groupings.”

The agency announced in 2015 it would no longer conduct or fund invasive research involving chimpanzees following outrage from animal rights activists calling to protect the endangered species.

Chimps were used historically for biomedical research on diseases such as HIV, hepatitis and cancer due to their biological similarities to humans. Scientists used the primates to study viruses and test the safety of medical treatments — including pharmaceutical drugs and radiation — until the NIH suspended funding for the practice in 2011.

The agency then pledged to retire all government-owned animals to sanctuaries, citing an independent assessment of the usefulness of chimpanzees for biomedical research and the designation of all chimps as endangered under the Endangered Species Act in 2015.

“We find no evidence that there is a need to continue to do research of an invasive sort on chimpanzees, not now and not going to in the future,” then-NIH Director Francis S. Collins said at the time.

Since then, more than 200 chimpanzees have been relocated to Chimp Haven in Keithville, Louisiana. At Chimp Haven, the animals live in large, forested areas and social groups designed to resemble their natural habitats.

“This has been a long road and something that many people thought would never happen,” Kathleen Conlee, vice president of animal research issues at Humane World for Animals, said in a statement to The New York Times . “It’s a really historic moment. This will be the end of the government’s use and confinement of chimps in labs.”

articles.title: Pennsylvania reports eighth measles-related death
articles.summary: Pennsylvania health officials and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) on Wednesday reported the commonwealth’s eighth measles-related death this year, one day after the U.S. lost its measles elimination status after 25 years. The state’s Department of Health said an unvaccinated Clinton County resident initially tested positive for the virus before their death.…
articles.body:
Pennsylvania health officials and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) on Wednesday reported the commonwealth’s eighth measles-related death this year, one day after the U.S. lost its measles elimination status after 25 years.

The state’s Department of Health said an unvaccinated Clinton County resident initially tested positive for the virus before their death.

Pennsylvania has seen 1,589 confirmed measles cases across 46 counties, with 28 confirmed cases as of Monday and 315 hospitalizations.

“Getting vaccinated remains the best protection against the measles virus; the vaccine is 97 percent effective at preventing measles for life after two doses,” the department said in a statement.

The Keystone State accounts for more than 1 in 4 cases reported in the entire country, according to the state’s dashboard .

Measles has made a resurgence as vaccination rates have declined. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) had been locked in a bitter dispute with Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a long-time vaccine skeptic, and accused him of “spreading misinformation.” Kennedy said there was no evidence of that.

The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) announced on Tuesday that measles was endemic in the U.S., Mexico and Bolivia following a three-day meeting with officials from all three countries. Countries that lose the elimination status must submit a corrective action plan to PAHO in order to regain the status.

Officials with the Trump administration have sought to downplay the significance of losing measles elimination status. Kennedy assured that the outbreak will be stopped and said the COVID-19 pandemic “disrupted” childhood immunizations.

CDC Director Erica Schwartz said that losing the elimination status will not change the federal response to the outbreaks, which has been criticized for being tepid . Administration officials have faced calls for a more robust measles vaccination campaign at the national level, but have questioned the safety and efficacy of the vaccine.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) on Monday cast blame at Kennedy and President Trump for the U.S. losing its elimination status.

“The resurgence of this dangerous virus is a direct consequence of the pathological stupidity plaguing this administration,” Schumer said.

Trump in August signed an executive order recommending the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine be split into three separate shots. He claimed without evidence that together the vaccine is “quite lethal.”

articles.title: Palmer Luckey warns AI-powered cyberattacks are outpacing defenses: 'It's time to start running' | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The Anduril co-founder says outdated technology is leaving systems vulnerable to a new wave of AI-enabled attacks.
articles.body:
AI-powered cyberattacks are moving faster than outdated technology systems can defend against them, Palmer Luckey warned at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday. Addressing the recent spate of tech outages, the Oculus founder and Anduril Industries co-founder argued that older systems are struggling to keep pace with the new hacking capabilities enabled by AI and warned it was time to quicken the pace of securing our defenses.

“We’re seeing the natural effects of a lot of these advanced AI tools allowing for the creation of various exploits,” he said.

While government officials largely attributed the latest set of technical issues to companies rushing to patch their systems to protect against the new vulnerabilities AI has discovered, Luckey focused on the underlying security challenges facing organizations using outdated technology.

Luckey explained that U.S. adversaries are currently exploiting the mismatch between new attack capabilities and our defense capabilities. These attacks are being carried out for both strategic and financial reasons, and North Korea was particularly involved, he added.

The interviewer, Andrew Ross Sorkin, noted that U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance had canceled his appearance at the Times’ conference this week because of the recent tech outages, saying he now had to attend meetings about the matter.

Given the situation, Sorkin asked Luckey how worried we should be about all this.

“It depends on how well prepared you are,” was Luckey’s answer. (He then ominously warned, “You guys are going to find out what’s going on soon enough.”)

The tech executive argued that AI could ultimately give defenders the upper hand, but they’d have to move more quickly.

“In the long run, the advantages are going to accrue to the side that is most effectively using AI for defense,” Luckey said. “With the people who say that everything can be hacked — they are right, for now. That actually may be the case with certain new techniques that are coming along. But as of right now, there’s a mismatch between the attackers who are very fast-moving and using technology and old, outdated systems that are not able to adopt technology as quickly as it is developed,” Luckey continued.

“And I think … people are going to have to pick up the pace,” he said. “It’s time to start running.”

articles.title: Palmer Luckey doesn’t deny that he’s a prepper
articles.summary: The Anduril founder said Wednesday that Americans should always have three days of food, water, and medicine — just in case.
articles.body:
Defense mogul Palmer Luckey — whose $90 billion drone and weapons startup Anduril is flush with government contracts — is still the kind of guy who prepares for the worst.

During Luckey’s conversation with Andrew Ross Sorkin at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit on Wednesday, the billionaire implied that Americans should batten down the hatches in case there are rough times ahead. Luckey himself has taken steps to prepare for a potential cataclysmic event, he said.

The conversation took place against the backdrop of a series of recent large-scale outages — at Apple , at Microsoft , at the NSA , and at the Federal Aviation Administration — that have led to concerns that America may be under attack by cyberthreat actors. The government has said that this is not the case , but Luckey cryptically teased that there may be more to the story.

“Look, all the 4chan schizo posters are like 12 hours ahead of the mainstream media on this. You guys are going to find out what’s going on soon enough,” he said.

Sorkin also asked Luckey to expound on comments made backstage “about what might be a cyber war that seems to be going on around us.”

Luckey described a “mismatch” between the sophisticated AI-powered cyberattacks that exist today and “old, outdated systems that are not able to adopt technology as quickly as it is developed.” He added: “I think people are going to have to pick up the pace. It’s time to start running.”

“What does that mean? Are you a prepper?” Sorkin asked.

Luckey didn’t deny the characterization. “I own a missile base 200 feet underground,” he answered, to audience laughter. “It’s a funny joke, but a missile base is actually a pretty bad way to run from the apocalypse. Everyone knows exactly where you are, and they [bases] are designed to take a hit from a nuclear weapon, a blast overpressure event.”

However, he had some qualifications on the prepper label. “The point is, like everyone should have three days of water. Everyone should have three days of dry food. If you have prescription medication, don’t go refill it when you run out. Make sure you refill it 72 hours before you run out.”

“People used to be taught this in middle school, and now everyone who remembers that is treated like a nut,” he added.

It should be pointed out that preparing for the apocalypse is not necessarily a new interest for Luckey. In 2017, a person familiar with the billionaire described him as a “prepper” and the bunker that was broached Wednesday is one of several decommissioned Cold War era underground bases that Luckey has purchased over the years. In 2024, he revealed that his massive video game collection is housed in one of them.

articles.title: Democrats skip a vote on adding Brendan Carr’s adviser to the FCC
articles.summary: Democrats boycotted a Senate committee confirmation vote for Danielle Thumann Severs to serve on the Federal Communications Commission.
articles.body: Senate commerce committee Chair Ted Cruz (R-TX) began a meeting Wednesday meant to confirm President Donald Trump’s nominee to the Federal Communications Commission with a lopsided dais. To his right sat all 14 Republican members of the panel, including Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD). To his left were about a dozen empty chairs — every Democratic member of the panel was absent. Cruz said he’d learned the night before that Democrats intended to boycott the vote, though Democrats say they’d repeatedly raised their concerns about advancing a Republican FCC nominee without a Democratic one. “The administration has shown it’s willing to move Democrats,” Cruz said, pointing to Senate votes scheduled on bipartisan pairs of nominations to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and the Securities and Exchange Commission. And even though the Supreme Court confirmed his power to do so, Cruz said, Trump has not moved to fire any Democrats from the FCC, as he did at the Federal Trade Commission. “This is an ordinary nomination to fill a vacancy previously held by someone in the same party,” Cruz said. But in statements and comments to reporters outside the committee room, Democrats said that the process has been far from normal. Senate committees often vote on nominations to historically independent agencies in bipartisan pairs. Confirming Danielle Thumann Severs, senior counsel to FCC Chair Brendan Carr, to become a commissioner at the agency would put the FCC at four total members — three Republicans and one Democrat, Anna Gomez. Gomez’s term has technically expired, though she can remain on the commission through next year unless she’s replaced. But Democrats fear that by confirming a third Republican to the FCC, Trump might finally fire Gomez, because he’d no longer need her present for a quorum to vote on key actions. Democrats asked for Thumann’s confirmation vote to be withheld until her nomination could be paired with a Democratic nomination. One way to do that would be to renominate Gomez. But so far, the president has not offered any Democratic nominees for the commission. Democrats said they made their concerns clear to Cruz, and added, “This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.” The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In addition to the procedural concerns, Democrats worry about Thumann’s work as an adviser to Carr, and whether she was truthful about the matters she worked on. In a letter asking Cruz to delay her confirmation vote, Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-NM) detailed his concerns. At the November 10th hearing where Thumann answered committee members’ questions, she testified that she had “not worked with the Chairman on any media-related issues,” Luján noted in the letter. But documents obtained via a Freedom of Information Act request show that Thumann was “looped in” on various media matters, and “helped draft Skydance’s commitments that facilitated the 2 FCC’s approval of the Skydance-Paramount merger,” Luján wrote. “She also played a role in processing informal complaints related to CBS 60 Minutes alleged news distortion and she apparently orchestrated the Commission’s response to consumers regarding the Jimmy Kimmel controversy.” The FCC did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the matter. Even Cruz admitted concerns with Carr’s handling of Kimmel’s comments in the aftermath of conservative activist Charlie Kirk’s killing. But at Wednesday’s meeting, he said he “emphatically agree[s]” that Thumann had resolved any lingering worries about that. He added that his JAWBONE Act, which the committee previously passed, could directly address First Amendment violations by government agencies of either party. The bill would let individuals sue government officials if they illegally try to compel social media or broadcast companies to remove their speech. Sen. Jerry Moran (R-KS), who’d similarly expressed concern over the Kimmel incident, said he found Thumann’s responses on the subject “comforting,” including in a phone call earlier that morning where he said he’d expressed his “serious interest in how the FCC protects and promotes free speech, including free speech on broadcast.” On the call, he said, “she was able to satisfy me once again in her answers, including an explanation for her role at the FCC and her lack of engagement on this type of issue as the FCC made decisions.” Speaking to reporters outside of the hearing room ahead of the meeting, Luján accused Thumann of lying to the committee. “The questions that I have is if she was lying about this, what else is she lying about and what else is she hiding?” he said. Luján said he wants both Thumann and Carr to appear before the committee by the end of the year to answer lawmakers’ questions. Asked if he’d support using the committee’s subpoena power or even pursuing impeachment against Carr when Democrats regain power next year, Luján said his vote to confirm Carr as a commissioner under President Joe Biden is among his biggest regrets, and that while he hopes Carr will testify voluntarily, “everything should be on the table here to be able to get answers for the American people.” When it came time to vote on whether to advance Thumann’s nomination for a final step of a vote on the Senate floor, all 15 Republicans voted “aye.” That gave Thumann enough votes for her nomination to advance to the Senate floor, where it’s expected to pass along party lines once scheduled. Still, the clerk listed off the names of the 13 Democratic committee members whose seats remained empty. There was no response.

articles.title: Top Republican says $350 billion defense reconciliation topline is ‘not gonna happen’
articles.summary: Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Ala.), the chairman of the House Armed Services Committee (HASC), poured cold water on Wednesday on the Pentagon’s $350 billion defense reconciliation topline ask during a Hudson Institute event in Washington, D.C. on Wednesday. “By the way, [$]350 [billion] is not gonna to happen. You may have guessed that, but a reconciliation bill…
articles.body:
Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Ala.), the chairman of the House Armed Services Committee (HASC), poured cold water on Wednesday on the Pentagon’s $350 billion defense reconciliation topline ask during a Hudson Institute event in Washington, D.C. on Wednesday.

“By the way, [$]350 [billion] is not gonna to happen. You may have guessed that, but a reconciliation bill is still possible. It’s going to have to be skinny down to deal with first and foremost the hole in the defense budget that Venezuela and Iran have created,” Rogers, a House defense hawk, said.

Rogers, who will not seek a waiver to remain top Republican on HASC next year, said if the Trump administration can slim down the request from $350 billion down to “100 [billion] or somewhere in that nature, there is a path for that.”

With doing that, it would be easier to move over the “essential” programs from the reconciliation portion into the baseline Pentagon budget request, which is set at $1.15 trillion, Rogers said.

The comments come as President Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth have been pressing Congress to push through the $350 billion package, which includes $17 billion for the Golden Dome missile defense system, $47 billion for expanded munitions production and $48 billion for critical minerals.

A week ago, the president publicly called on the Senate to pass the reconciliation funding as the time runs out for the Republican majority in Congress.

“I rebuilt our Military in my First Term, and we’re doing it AGAIN, bigger and better than ever before! The Radical Democrat Majority in the next Congress has already made it clear that their Number One Agenda is to BLOCK and RESIST this historic investment in our National Security,” Trump wrote.

Republican senators have warned that the president’s push for GOP leaders to rely on budget reconciliation process to ram through $350 billion in Pentagon funding could risk a government shutdown, The Hill previously reported. The looming deadline to keep the government open is Dec. 11.

The Pentagon has continued to call on Capitol Hill to greenlight the request, arguing it is paramount for strengthening the military and safeguarding U.S. national security.

Pentagon Deputy Secretary Steve Feinberg was at the Senate GOP lunch on Wednesday, according to one GOP source. He discussed the $350 billion request, according to two other sources familiar with the matter.

Later in the day, he huddled with senators in the Senate Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility (SCIF) to continue those discussions. But the effort has not brought a breakthrough.

Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) described the internal discussion as a “jump-ball.”

“Everybody recognizes it’s going to be a Herculean effort to get the House and the Senate in terms of the scope and the process,” Cornyn told reporters after leaving the meeting.

Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) said the conversations are ongoing, but noted he is for moving the $350 billion package.

“Probably not this week, but again, we are not taking it off the table at all,” Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wisc.) told reporters when asked about reconciliation plans.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said earlier this morning he aims to make a decision on if Republicans will move forward with a time-consuming budget reconciliation to fund the Pentagon after the GOP’s Wednesday lunch meeting.

articles.title: Former cybersecurity director: Tech outages ‘ultimately a good news story’
articles.summary: Chris Krebs, the former director of the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, on Wednesday said that the recent spate of technology outages from the past week are “ultimately a good news story.” “I know it kind of sucks in the moment when you can’t access your app or your flights are delayed, but we’re…
articles.body:
Chris Krebs, the former director of the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, on Wednesday said that the recent spate of technology outages from the past week are “ultimately a good news story.”

“I know it kind of sucks in the moment when you can’t access your app or your flights are delayed, but we’re finding vulnerabilities,” Krebs told CNN’s Jake Tapper. “We’re finding bugs, we’re fixing them before our adversaries find them themselves and bring a network down intentionally.”

Americans have seen a wave of outages affecting businesses like Microsoft and Apple, as well as an outage that paused all internal communications at the National Security Agency (NSA). An outage likely caused by a router at a radio facility in Arkansas prompted the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to issue a nationwide ground stop of all flights, the third in the last 25 years.

Krebs said he agreed with Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who both said there was no evidence suggesting these outages were caused by cyberattacks.

“If it was the Chinese, they’d either burn that network to the ground or they’d be in there,” Krebs told Tapper. “You’d never know they were there. So cyberattacks tend to be either very visible or very stealthy, not this muddy middle area.”

Outages that affected the FAA and Apple occurred amid updates or upgrades to their software. Krebs said that companies using frontier AI models from tech companies like OpenAI and Anthropic have those models find bugs and patch them.

He also emphasized how it’s “human nature to string things together” regarding the frequency of these outages, but said “it’s a coincidence.”

Krebs said he expects to see more outages in the future but said “we just kind of need to take a breath, take a beat and realize that it’s not the end of the world,” noting how these recent outages lasted mere hours and not several days.

Tapper noted how people have stockpiled food and water in response to these incidents, and asked Krebs what he tells them. He replied that emergency plans should always be in place, whether in preparation for a wildfire in Los Angeles, a hurricane in Florida, a tornado in the Midwest or a winter storm in the Midatlantic and Northeast.

President Trump ousted Krebs from his previous role after affirming that 2020 election, where Trump lost reelection, was secure.

The rash of outages and digital disruptions over the past week have raised questions about potential vulnerabilities to large-scale cybersecurity. Mullin suggested it could have been caused by super intelligence (SI), the Trump administration’s preferred term for artificial intelligence.

But lawmakers have questioned the coincidence of these disruptions, with some Republicans urging Trump to address Americans at how the White House will respond.

Trump told reporters Tuesday that “ it’s fine ” when it comes to this incidents, adding that “things like that happen.”

articles.title: Users report PlayStation issues hours before ‘GTA VI’ drop
articles.summary: “GTV VI” is scheduled to release at midnight on Thursday, though players in some parts of the world were already granted access as midnight arrived in their regions.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – The Playstation Network appears to be operating as normal after a brief spike in reported outages on Wednesday.

The outage reports also came just hours before the release of “Grand Theft Auto VI,” one of the most anticipated video games in years.

“They better fix [this] before it drops man,” one Reddit user wrote amid the reported issues, which allegedly included difficulties signing into the Playstation Network, and users getting locked out.

DownDetector had recorded thousands of reports of outages, with spikes starting after 1 p.m. EST. PlayStation’s status page, meanwhile, says all services are currently up and running.

A representative for PlayStation was not immediately available to comment.

“GTV VI” is scheduled to release at midnight on Thursday, though players in some parts of the world were already granted access as midnight arrived in their regions. New Zealand was among the first countries where players could access the game, and internet providers prepared for a surge in downloads as midnight approached.

“The game file size at 212 gigabytes is unprecedented,” said Kurt Rodgers, network strategy manager for Chorus New Zealand. “That’s more than a quarter of the average household’s data usage in an entire month, all in one go.”

As of 5 p.m. ET, it appeared outage reports had dipped to about 1,300.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Navy peacoat retired after over a century
articles.summary: The iconic dark blue uniform worn by the U.S. Navy since 1897 retires next October after over a century of service and fashion.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — The iconic dark blue uniform worn by the U.S. Navy since 1897 will retire next October after more than a century of service and style.

A “seabag reduction” plan changes the U.S. Navy’s official uniform options as it seeks to simplify required uniform items, reducing the number of clothing items sailors must buy and maintain, reports the Maritime Executive.

The Navy has worn the peacoat since the 1800s, taking the style from the British Royal Navy, whose sailors wore the coat as far back as 1731 . Since adopting the wool coat stateside, American civilians have joined naval officers in sporting the peacoat, which remains a popular winter-weather fashion staple.

The U.S. Navy stopped issuing the peacoats in 2020 and has been trying to phase out the coat since 2017.

Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle also announced intended improvements to uniform quality with the new policy, which also introduces a new digital app that lets sailors customize their new uniforms with insignia.

The dinner dress white jacket and acrylic V-neck will also be phased out, and sailors will wear their dinner dress blue jackets year-round. Physical training uniforms will ditch the gold shirts and switch to a blue-on-blue ensemble.

articles.title: Frozen dessert bars recalled over undeclared allergens
articles.summary: So far, no illnesses have been reported in connection with the recalled product.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — A California company is recalling its frozen chocolate banana dessert after a packaging error led to potentially undeclared allergens.

Naia Inc. is recalling its Chocolate Banana Bar Sorbetto with code dates between Oct. 5 and Oct. 8, 2027, because it may contain undeclared pistachios, milk and eggs, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration announced this week.

The recalled desserts were available between Oct. 7 and Nov. 13, 2026, at retail grocery stores, supermarkets and other retailers in Northern California and Reno, Nevada.

The company initiated the recall after realizing that its “Pistachio Bar Gelato bars were packaged in wrappers labeled as Chocolate Banana Bar Sorbetto,” according to the FDA.

Consumers should return the dessert to the place of purchase for a refund and contact the company at (510) 724-2479 with any questions. So far, no illnesses have been reported in connection with the recalled product.

Republican lawmakers are offering mixed reactions to President Trump’s warm embrace of Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin ahead of the three leaders’ upcoming meeting.

Some view the theatrical trilateral as a poor signal of where U.S. priorities lie , while others defend an American leader open to having tough conversations with powerful countries.

“I’ve never been successful in getting inside the president’s head, but I can tell you where I am, we have to be more clear about who our friends are and who our allies are,” said Sen. Joh Curtis (R-Utah), a member of the Senate Foreign Relations and Senate Judiciary Committee.

articles.title: Iran’s ‘dirty bomb’ threat underscores risks to US homeland
articles.summary: A reported plot by Iran to target Washington, D.C., with a so-called “dirty bomb” has brought fears of an attack on the U.S. homeland to the forefront this week. Coming on the heels of two men arrested late last month for a suspected Iran-linked terror plot on a U.S.-run airbase in the United Kingdom, experts…
articles.body:
A reported plot by Iran to target Washington, D.C., with a so-called “dirty bomb” has brought fears of an attack on the U.S. homeland to the forefront this week.

Coming on the heels of two men arrested late last month for a suspected Iran-linked terror plot on a U.S.-run airbase in the United Kingdom, experts say Iran appears to be looking for options to impose costs on the U.S. as President Trump’s war on the country stretches on.

“These threats have substantially increased. Our women and men abroad, our women and men here in the United States, are under greater threat,” Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told lawmakers Wednesday of Iran, during a House worldwide threats hearing.

Other officials have downplayed the CNN report, which cited intelligence that Iran was planning to target senior Trump administration officials using materials already in the U.S.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Tuesday that “the homeland is secure,” and Iran’s planning was “aspirational” and not a “new threat.”

Speaking during a House Homeland Security Committee hearing, Clayton would not comment on CNN’s reporting, only saying that the U.S. remains committed “to detecting, deterring, and combating the Iranian lethal plotting outside the United States and inside the United States.”

Brian Haggerty, a former senior analyst at the Central Intelligence Agency who focused on Middle East security issues, said America has “been worried about the threat of a dirty bomb in a major metropolitan U.S. city” since before the 9/11 attacks.

“In that sense, there’s nothing new about the threat,” Haggerty, who is now with the Defense Priorities think tank, told The Hill.

And since the first Trump administration, Iran has plotted against current and former U.S. officials — most plans concentrated on attacking individuals while they were traveling overseas — including a murder-for-hire plot against Trump himself in 2024.

But Haggerty noted that Tehran is “looking for options right now” to impose costs on the U.S. to make it harder for Washington to continue a blockade on Iranian ports in the Strait of Hormuz, a military operation that has crippled Tehran’s economy and has been in place since summer. The wider war is now nearing the nine-month mark.

“They don’t want to return to full-scale war right now. That’s not what they’re looking to do,” he said. “An attack like a dirty bomb on U.S. soil . . . it would really have to be in response to something much more threatening to Tehran to warrant something like that.”

Instead, “they’re looking in other domains. It’s called horizontal escalation,” Haggerty added. “Iran can’t outdo us militarily. But maybe in a different domain like cyber or assassination or something like that, they can strike us in this other area to impose greater costs and make it harder for us to continue on our current trajectory of holding the blockade.”

These asymmetrical threats impose a cost on the U.S. simply by forcing the government and military to increase measures to guard against such a scenario.

Case in point, CNN reported that the dirty bomb plotting picked up by U.S. intelligence, which included very specific locations and targets, set off a flurry of contingency planning in Washington.

Other intelligence suggesting Tehran may use chemical weapons against U.S. service members, diplomatic and intelligence personnel stationed in the Middle East reportedly prompted a separate planning effort to make sure Americans there have the necessary equipment and training to protect themselves.

And the U.S. was forced to quickly move its aircraft from two airfields in the U.K. after five men were initially arrested on Sept. 27 for a suspected terror plot on the RAF Fairford air base in Gloucestershire, England.

American B-1 bombers positioned at RAF Fairford to strike Iran were moved in October.

Another 13 American aircraft stationed at RAF Mildenhall were spotted departing for bases elsewhere in Europe earlier this month due to a threat related to Iran, The Wall Street Journal first reported.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said at the time that the United States is “constantly repositioning forces around the world for a variety of reasons.”

The longer the Iran war stretches, the greater the chance that such threats escalate, according to Mona Yacoubian, director of the Middle East Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) think tank.

“A prolonged war heightens the prospects for all types of escalation — cyber, assassinations, drones and other asymmetric capabilities,” she told The Hill. “We’ve already seen increased reporting of Iranian intent/desire to undertake such attacks, for example on U.S. fighter jets at UK military bases.”

But she was in a similar mindset as Haggerty that Iran’s intent is not necessarily to provoke wider war.

“A ‘dirty bomb’ in the U.S. would signal a significant uptick in Iranian capabilities, which seems unlikely at this time,” Yacoubian said.
